title: CISA Manual · Study Guide
edition: Follows the structure of the CISA Review Manual, 28th edition. Original summaries, not the manual text.

sections.title: IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, Functions and Codes of Ethics
sections.summary: Sets the professional rules every IS auditor works under: ISACA’s IT Audit Framework (ITAF), the Code of Professional Ethics, and how the audit function is organised and given authority through a charter.
points: ITAF standards are mandatory; guidelines explain how to apply them; tools and techniques give practical examples.
Standards are grouped as general (independence, objectivity, proficiency, due care), performance (planning, risk assessment, evidence, using the work of others) and reporting.
The audit charter defines purpose, authority, responsibility and accountability, and is approved by the board or audit committee.
Internal audit reports functionally to the audit committee and administratively to senior management to protect independence.
The Code of Professional Ethics requires due care, objectivity, confidentiality, competence and support for standards; breaches can lead to disciplinary action.

terms.d: ISACA’s IT Audit Framework: the set of mandatory standards plus supporting guidelines and techniques.
Formal document that establishes the audit function’s mandate and unrestricted access.
Being free of relationships that a reasonable third party would see as compromising objectivity.

auditor: Confirm the charter exists, is approved at board level and is reviewed periodically.
Check reporting lines and whether auditors have assessed and disclosed any impairment.
traps: The auditor never approves or implements controls; doing so impairs independence.
When independence is impaired, disclose it; do not simply continue.

sections.title: Types of Audits, Assessments and Reviews
sections.summary: Explains the different engagements an IS auditor may perform and how audits differ from assessments and reviews, including reliance on third-party assurance reports.
points: Audit types include compliance, financial, operational, integrated, administrative, IS, specialised and forensic audits.
An integrated audit combines financial, operational and IS audit work to assess controls across a business process.
Assessments (e.g. risk or control self-assessments) are often less formal and may be performed by management.
Third-party service audits (e.g. SOC 1 / SOC 2 reports) let user organisations rely on a provider’s controls; check report type, period and exceptions.
Forensic audits collect evidence for possible legal action and must protect chain of custody.

terms.d: Type 1 covers control design at a point in time; Type 2 also tests operating effectiveness over a period.
A single engagement covering financial, operational and IT controls together.

auditor: When relying on another auditor’s report, evaluate their independence, competence, scope and period covered.
Review complementary user entity controls the client must operate.
traps: A Type 1 report gives no assurance that controls worked over time.
A SOC report outside your audit period needs bridge letters or extra testing.

sections.title: Risk-Based Audit Planning
sections.summary: Shows how auditors plan engagements and the annual plan around risk, so effort goes where the organisation is most exposed.
points: Start by understanding business objectives, processes, IT environment and applicable laws and regulations.
Audit risk = inherent risk × control risk × detection risk; auditors manage detection risk through the nature, timing and extent of testing.
Risk-based planning prioritises high-risk areas and documents why areas are in or out of scope.
Materiality in IS audit considers both monetary amount and non-monetary impact (e.g. safety, reputation, regulatory breach).
Risk assessment techniques range from qualitative scoring to quantitative models; results drive the audit plan and resource allocation.

terms.d: Risk before any controls are considered.
Risk that controls will not prevent or detect a material error.
Risk that audit procedures will not detect a material error.

auditor: Revisit the risk assessment when significant change occurs (new systems, incidents, regulations).
Link each audit objective to a specific risk.
traps: The auditor cannot change inherent or control risk, only detection risk.
The first step in planning is understanding the business, not choosing tests.

sections.title: Types of Controls and Considerations
sections.summary: Describes control classifications, control objectives and how general and application controls work together.
points: Controls are preventive, detective or corrective; also deterrent, compensating and recovery in some models.
Control objectives state what a control must achieve (e.g. only authorised changes reach production).
IT general controls (access, change, operations, backup) support the reliability of application controls.
Application controls cover input, processing and output; automated controls are tested once if ITGCs are effective.
Compensating controls reduce risk when a primary control (e.g. segregation of duties) cannot be applied.

terms.d: An alternative control that reduces the risk left by a missing or weak primary control.
IT general controls over the environment in which applications run.

auditor: Test ITGCs before relying on automated application controls.
Assess control design first, then operating effectiveness.
traps: Preventive controls are generally preferred, but the BEST answer depends on the risk described.
Review of logs is detective, not preventive.

sections.title: Audit Project Management
sections.summary: Covers running an audit as a project: objectives, scope, work program, resources, schedule, supervision and communication.
points: Define audit objectives and scope, then design the audit program (procedures to collect evidence).
Plan resources and skills; use specialists where needed and supervise their work.
Agree timing and logistics with auditee management; hold an opening meeting.
Monitor progress, document work papers and review them before conclusions are drawn.

terms.d: The step-by-step procedures to achieve audit objectives.
Documented evidence of planning, procedures, results and conclusions.

auditor: Check work papers support every finding and are reviewed by a senior auditor.
traps: Scope changes requested by the auditee must be assessed for independence impact and documented.

sections.title: Audit Testing and Sampling Methodology
sections.summary: Explains compliance versus substantive testing and how to use statistical and non-statistical sampling.
points: Compliance tests check whether controls operate as designed; substantive tests check the accuracy of data and balances.
Attribute sampling estimates rates (used for compliance testing); variable sampling estimates amounts (substantive).
Stop-or-go sampling stops early when few errors are expected; discovery sampling checks for at least one occurrence (e.g. fraud).
Sample size rises with confidence level and expected error rate, and falls as tolerable error rises.
Statistical sampling allows the risk of sampling error to be quantified; judgmental sampling does not.

terms.d: Maximum error rate or amount the auditor will accept and still conclude a control is effective.
Probability that the sample results represent the population.
Dividing a population into groups with similar characteristics to improve sampling efficiency.

auditor: Choose sampling based on the test objective; document the method so results can be defended.
traps: When controls are weak, increase substantive testing rather than relying on compliance tests.
Use statistical sampling when an objective, defensible conclusion is needed.

sections.title: Audit Evidence Collection Techniques
sections.summary: Describes what makes evidence sufficient and reliable and the techniques used to gather it.
points: Evidence must be sufficient, reliable, relevant and useful to support conclusions.
Reliability is higher for independent sources, evidence obtained directly by the auditor, and objective system data.
Techniques: inquiry, observation, inspection of documents, reperformance, analytical procedures, CAATs, interviews and walk-throughs.
Preserve and protect evidence; maintain chain of custody when legal action is possible.

terms.d: The auditor independently executes a control or calculation to verify results.
Documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence and when.

auditor: Corroborate verbal evidence with documents or system data.
traps: Evidence from the auditee is less reliable than evidence the auditor obtains directly.
Observation is reliable only for the moment it occurred.

sections.title: Audit Data Analytics
sections.summary: Shows how data analytics, CAATs and continuous auditing extend coverage and find anomalies across whole populations.
points: CAATs and generalised audit software test 100% of transactions to find duplicates, gaps, outliers and exceptions.
Continuous auditing techniques: embedded audit modules (SCARF), integrated test facility, snapshots, audit hooks, continuous and intermittent simulation.
Data must be extracted completely and accurately; validate record counts and totals before analysis.
Analytics also support risk assessment and fraud detection; algorithms must be documented and tested.

terms.d: Integrated test facility: fictitious entity processed alongside live data.
Assurance provided simultaneously with, or shortly after, the events it covers.

auditor: Confirm data integrity and access controls over the audit data copy.
traps: ITF test data must be reversed so it does not affect real results.
Continuous auditing suits high-volume automated environments.

sections.title: Reporting and Communication Techniques
sections.summary: Covers communicating results: exit meetings, report structure, rating findings and follow-up.
points: Discuss findings with auditee management before issuing the report to confirm facts.
Report findings with condition, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation, plus management’s response.
Rate findings by risk so priorities are clear; summarise for senior management and the audit committee.
Follow up to verify that agreed actions were implemented; escalate overdue high-risk items.

terms.d: Meeting to discuss findings and agree facts before the final report.
Process to confirm that corrective actions were implemented and effective.

auditor: Make sure every recommendation addresses the root cause, not just the symptom.
traps: The auditor must not drop a valid finding because management disagrees; report it with management’s view.

sections.title: Quality Assurance and Improvement of the Audit Process
sections.summary: Explains how the audit function assures its own quality through internal and external quality reviews and control self-assessment.
points: A quality assurance and improvement program includes ongoing supervision, periodic internal assessments and external reviews.
Control self-assessment (CSA) workshops let management and staff evaluate their own controls; auditors facilitate.
Audit methodology, training and tools should be updated as risks and technology change.

terms.d: Control self-assessment: management-led evaluation of controls, often in facilitated workshops.

auditor: Check that lessons learned from reviews are fed back into the audit methodology.
traps: CSA supplements internal audit; it does not replace it.

sections.title: Laws, Regulations and Industry Standards
sections.summary: How external obligations (laws, regulations, contracts and industry standards) shape IT governance and what the auditor checks.
points: Management must identify all applicable legal, regulatory and contractual requirements and assign owners.
Requirements are translated into policies and controls and monitored for ongoing compliance.
Industry standards (ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, NIST) may be mandatory by contract or adopted voluntarily.
Changes in laws must trigger review of policies, controls and contracts.

terms.d: Conforming with laws, regulations, contracts and internal policies.

auditor: Check there is a register of obligations with owners and evidence of monitoring.
traps: The first step is identifying which requirements apply, before testing compliance.

sections.title: Organizational Structure, IT Governance and IT Strategy
sections.summary: Explains governance of enterprise IT (GEIT), governance structures and committees, and how IT strategy is aligned to business strategy.
points: Governance (board) evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds, runs and monitors (COBIT 2019).
IT strategy committee (board level) advises on strategic alignment; IT steering committee (executive level) prioritises and oversees projects and investments.
IT strategy must derive from business strategy and be approved by senior management.
Organisational structure must support segregation of duties between development, operations, security and users.
Good practice frameworks: COBIT 2019, ISO/IEC 38500, ITIL; balanced scorecard for performance.

terms.d: Governance of enterprise IT: ensuring IT creates value, manages risk and uses resources in line with business goals.
Splitting incompatible duties so no single person can both commit and conceal an error or fraud.

auditor: Review committee charters, minutes and evidence that IT strategy is reviewed against business plans.
Check SoD conflicts in IT roles (e.g. developer with production access).
traps: Board-level oversight is the strategy committee; project prioritisation is the steering committee.
Strategy alignment is the PRIMARY objective of IT governance.

sections.title: IT Policies, Standards, Procedures and Guidelines
sections.summary: Describes the policy hierarchy and how policies are developed, approved, communicated and reviewed.
points: Policies state management intent and are approved by senior management/board; standards are mandatory specifics; procedures give steps; guidelines are advisory.
Policies must be communicated, acknowledged and periodically reviewed.
Lower-level policies must align with the enterprise information security policy.
Exceptions must be documented, risk-assessed and approved.

terms.d: Mandatory requirement that supports a policy (e.g. password length).
Recommended, non-mandatory practice.

auditor: Compare policies with regulations and good practice; test that procedures are followed in practice.
traps: An unapproved or outdated policy is a governance weakness even if staff follow it.

sections.title: Enterprise Architecture and Considerations
sections.summary: Explains enterprise architecture (EA) as the blueprint linking business, data, applications and technology.
points: EA documents current and target states and the roadmap between them.
Frameworks include Zachman and TOGAF; layers cover business, data, application and technology.
EA reduces duplication, supports standardisation and informs investment decisions.

terms.d: Structured description of how business processes, information and technology fit together.

auditor: Check projects are reviewed for compliance with the target architecture.
traps: EA is a planning and governance tool, not a technical diagram only.

sections.title: Enterprise Risk Management
sections.summary: Covers building a risk management program: context, identification, analysis, treatment, monitoring and reporting.
points: A risk management program needs objectives, scope, roles, risk appetite and reporting set by senior management.
Process: identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities; assess likelihood and impact; treat; monitor and communicate.
Treatment options: mitigate, transfer/share, avoid, accept within appetite.
Risk registers track owners, ratings, treatments and residual risk; risk is reassessed after significant change.

terms.d: The amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
Risk remaining after treatment.

auditor: Check risks are linked to business objectives and that acceptance is signed off by authorised owners.
traps: Risk acceptance is a management decision, never the auditor’s.

sections.title: Data Privacy Program and Principles
sections.summary: Explains how organisations manage personal data across its lifecycle and comply with privacy laws.
points: Privacy principles: lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability, individual rights.
Privacy impact assessments (PIAs/DPIAs) identify privacy risk early in new systems or changes.
Roles include data protection officer and data owners; third parties processing data need contracts.
Breach notification requirements must be built into incident response.

terms.d: Privacy impact assessment: structured review of privacy risk in a process or system.

auditor: Check data inventories, consent records, retention schedules and PIA evidence.
traps: Privacy (rights over personal data) is not the same as confidentiality (protection from disclosure).

sections.title: Data Governance and Classification
sections.summary: Covers managing data as an asset: ownership, quality, lifecycle and classification.
points: Data owners classify data by sensitivity and criticality and approve access.
Classification drives handling, encryption, retention and disposal requirements.
Data quality dimensions include accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness.
Data lifecycle: create, store, use, share, archive, destroy.

terms.d: Business person accountable for a data set’s classification and access.
IT role that implements the owner’s requirements.

auditor: Test that classification labels are applied and controls match the class.
traps: Classification is the owner’s responsibility, not IT’s.

sections.title: IT Resource Management
sections.summary: Covers managing IT people, budgets, investments and assets for value.
points: IT investment decisions use business cases and portfolio management.
HR practices: hiring checks, training, job rotation, mandatory leave, termination procedures.
Financial management: budgeting, cost allocation/chargeback, tracking benefits.

terms.d: Charging IT costs to the business units that consume services.

auditor: Check key-person dependencies, training plans and termination access removal.
traps: Mandatory leave and rotation are detective controls for fraud.

sections.title: IT Vendor Management
sections.summary: Explains sourcing strategies and managing third parties across the contract lifecycle.
points: Sourcing options: insourcing, outsourcing, cloud, onshore/offshore, hybrid.
Due diligence before selection; contracts with SLAs, security, right-to-audit, data ownership, exit and subcontracting clauses.
Ongoing monitoring of performance and risk; independent assurance reports (e.g. SOC 2).
Accountability for risk remains with the organisation.

terms.d: Contract term allowing the customer or its auditors to audit the vendor.

auditor: Review vendor risk assessments, SLA reports and how exceptions are followed up.
traps: Outsourcing transfers the activity, not the accountability.

sections.title: IT Performance Monitoring and Reporting
sections.summary: Covers measuring IT performance with KPIs, KRIs and balanced scorecards and reporting to governance bodies.
points: KPIs measure performance; KRIs give early warning of rising risk.
The IT balanced scorecard links IT measures to business goals across several perspectives.
Maturity/capability models assess process improvement.
Metrics must be relevant, reliable and reported to the right audience.

terms.d: Key risk indicator: metric signalling increased risk exposure.

auditor: Test the accuracy of reported metrics back to source data.
traps: Metrics that are not aligned to business objectives have little governance value.

sections.title: Quality Assurance and Quality Management of IT
sections.summary: Explains quality management systems and QA for IT processes and products.
points: QA checks adherence to processes and standards; quality control tests products.
ISO 9001 quality management; continuous improvement (plan-do-check-act).
QA should be independent of the teams it reviews.

terms.d: Activities that ensure processes are followed to produce quality outcomes.

auditor: Check QA reviews happen, are independent and lead to corrective action.
traps: QA is process-focused; QC is product-focused.

chapters.title: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation

sections.title: Project Governance and Management
sections.summary: Covers portfolio, program and project management, project roles, planning techniques and project control.
points: Portfolio management selects and balances projects against strategy; programs group related projects.
Roles: sponsor (funding, accountability), steering committee (direction), project manager (delivery), users (requirements, acceptance), QA, security.
Planning tools: WBS, Gantt, critical path method, PERT, function point analysis, earned value.
Control scope with formal change requests; track time, cost and quality; manage project risk.
Close projects formally: acceptance, lessons learned, documentation handover.

terms.d: Longest sequence of dependent tasks; any delay delays the project.
Compares planned value, earned value and actual cost to measure progress.
Estimates software size from its functions (inputs, outputs, files, interfaces, inquiries).

auditor: Check governance gates, status reporting accuracy and change control over scope.
traps: Project sponsor owns the business case.
Scope creep without change control is a key risk.

sections.title: Business Case and Feasibility Analysis
sections.summary: Explains justifying investments and assessing technical, economic and operational feasibility.
points: The business case states the problem, options, costs, benefits, risks and alignment with strategy.
Feasibility covers technical, economic (ROI, NPV, payback), operational, legal and schedule factors.
The business case is revisited at phase gates; benefits are tracked after implementation.

terms.d: Return on investment: benefit relative to cost.

auditor: Check the business case was approved and updated when assumptions changed.
traps: A project that no longer meets its business case should be re-evaluated or stopped.

sections.title: System Development Methodologies
sections.summary: Compares SDLC approaches and acquisition options, and what controls each needs.
points: Waterfall: sequential phases with sign-offs; suits stable requirements.
Agile (e.g. Scrum): short iterations, user collaboration, working software; controls must be built into the process.
Other approaches: prototyping, RAD, DevOps/DevSecOps, object-oriented and component-based development, reverse/re-engineering.
Buying software: requirements, RFP, vendor evaluation, contract, escrow for source code.

terms.d: Third party holds vendor source code, released if the vendor fails.
Integrating security into automated development and operations pipelines.

auditor: Check requirements traceability, user involvement and security requirements in every approach.
traps: Lack of user involvement in requirements is a leading cause of failure.

sections.title: Control Identification and Design
sections.summary: Covers designing application controls: input, processing, output and data integrity.
points: Input controls: validation edits (sequence, limit, range, validity, reasonableness, check digit, completeness, duplicate, logical relationship).
Processing controls: run-to-run totals, reconciliation, edit checks on calculations, exception reports.
Output controls: distribution, balancing, secure handling and retention.
Data integrity: ACID properties, referential and relational integrity.

terms.d: Calculated digit appended to a number to detect transcription errors.
A transaction either completes fully or not at all.

auditor: Confirm controls are designed during development, not added after go-live.
traps: Hash totals detect missing or altered records; they have no business meaning.

sections.title: System Readiness and Implementation Testing
sections.summary: Explains testing levels and approaches before go-live.
points: Unit, integration/interface, system, acceptance (UAT and QAT) testing.
System testing includes recovery, security, load, volume, stress and performance testing.
Regression testing confirms changes did not break existing functions; parallel testing compares old and new systems.
Test data should be representative and protected; production data used in testing must be masked.

terms.d: User acceptance testing: users confirm the system meets business requirements.
Re-running tests to make sure changes did not introduce errors.

auditor: Check test plans, results, defect resolution and formal user sign-off.
traps: Users, not IT, sign off acceptance testing.

sections.title: Implementation Configuration and Release Management
sections.summary: Covers configuration baselines and controlled release into production.
points: Configuration management maintains approved baselines and versions (e.g. CMDB).
Releases are planned, tested, approved, scheduled and include rollback plans.
Migration to production is done by a function independent of developers.

terms.d: Approved configuration used as a reference for future changes.

auditor: Test that what is in production matches the approved release.
traps: Developers moving their own code to production breaks segregation of duties.

sections.title: System Migration, Infrastructure Deployment and Data Conversion
sections.summary: Explains changeover methods and controls over migrating data and infrastructure.
points: Changeover: parallel (safest), phased, pilot, abrupt/direct (riskiest).
Data conversion controls: record counts, control totals, reconciliation, error reports, user sign-off.
Fallback plans and backups are required before cutover.

terms.d: Running old and new systems together until the new one is proven.

auditor: Verify reconciliation of converted data and approval of exceptions.
traps: Data conversion without reconciliation is a major risk to data integrity.

sections.title: Postimplementation Review
sections.summary: Covers evaluating whether a project achieved its objectives and benefits after go-live.
points: PIR assesses benefits realisation, user satisfaction, controls and lessons learned.
Performed once the system has stabilised; independence of reviewers matters.
Results feed future projects and the portfolio process.

terms.d: Postimplementation review.

auditor: Compare actual results with the business case.
traps: A PIR too soon after go-live gives an incomplete picture.

chapters.title: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience

sections.title: IT Components
sections.summary: Introduces the hardware, software, network and cloud components an auditor must understand and their key risks.
points: Hardware: servers, storage, end-user devices; operating systems and middleware.
Networks: OSI/TCP-IP layers, LAN/WAN, wireless, routers, switches, firewalls.
Cloud and virtualisation change who operates which component (shared responsibility).
Hardware maintenance, monitoring and capacity reports support reliability.

terms.d: Seven-layer reference model: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.

auditor: Understand the components in scope before testing controls over them.
traps: Fibre optic is the most secure cable type against tapping.

sections.title: IT Asset Management
sections.summary: Covers knowing and managing every IT asset across its lifecycle.
points: Maintain a complete inventory of hardware, software and licences with owners.
Lifecycle: plan, acquire, deploy, maintain, retire, dispose securely.
Asset data feeds patching, risk assessment, licence compliance and incident response.

terms.d: Configuration management database: records configuration items and relationships.

auditor: Reconcile the inventory to network discovery results.
traps: Unknown assets cannot be secured or patched.

sections.title: Job Scheduling and Production Process Automation
sections.summary: Explains controlled, automated running of production jobs.
points: Scheduling tools run jobs in sequence with dependencies and restart points.
Changes to schedules follow change management; job logs and exceptions are reviewed.
Automation reduces manual error and improves reliability.

terms.d: Software that automatically runs production jobs on a defined schedule.

auditor: Check who can change job definitions and how failed jobs are handled.
traps: Unauthorized changes to job schedules can bypass program change controls.

sections.title: System Interfaces
sections.summary: Covers controls over data exchanged between systems.
points: Interfaces include file transfers, APIs, messaging and middleware.
Controls: inventory of interfaces with owners, reconciliation of counts and totals, error handling, encryption in transit, authentication.
Interface failures can silently corrupt or lose data.

terms.d: Application programming interface used for system-to-system communication.

auditor: Test reconciliations between source and target systems.
traps: Undocumented interfaces are a common source of unmanaged risk.

sections.title: End-User Computing and Shadow IT
sections.summary: Explains risks of user-developed tools and unapproved technology and how to control them.
points: End-user computing (spreadsheets, macros, small databases) can support critical decisions without IT controls.
Shadow IT: technology used without IT/security approval (often cloud SaaS).
Risks: data leakage, unpatched vulnerabilities, no backup, inaccurate results, compliance breaches.
Controls: policy and approval process, inventory of critical EUCs, IT as a service partner, procurement review, restricted admin rights, user education, monitoring (e.g. CASB).

terms.d: Systems or services used without the approval of IT or security.
End-user computing: applications built and run by business users.

auditor: Identify critical EUC tools and test their change, access and backup controls.
traps: Banning tools alone rarely works; providing approved alternatives is the better answer.

sections.title: Systems Availability and Capacity Management
sections.summary: Covers keeping services available and planning capacity for demand.
points: Availability management uses redundancy, clustering, load balancing and monitoring.
Capacity planning forecasts demand for processing, storage and network resources.
Performance reports and trend analysis prevent outages.

terms.d: Ensuring IT capacity meets current and future business needs cost-effectively.

auditor: Check capacity plans exist and are based on business forecasts.
traps: Reactive capacity upgrades indicate weak planning.

sections.title: Problem and Incident Management
sections.summary: Distinguishes restoring service quickly (incident) from removing root causes (problem).
points: Incident management: log, classify, prioritise, resolve or escalate, close.
Problem management: root cause analysis, known error records, permanent fixes.
Help desk metrics and trend analysis identify recurring problems.

terms.d: A problem with a documented root cause and workaround.

auditor: Check incidents are logged completely and recurring incidents trigger problem records.
traps: Root cause = problem management, not incident management.

sections.title: IT Change, Configuration and Patch Management
sections.summary: Explains controlling changes to production systems, configurations and patches.
points: Change process: request, assess impact, approve (e.g. CAB), test, implement, review.
Emergency changes are documented and approved retrospectively.
Patch management: inventory, prioritise by risk, test, deploy, verify.
Segregate development, test and production environments.

terms.d: Change advisory board that assesses and approves changes.

auditor: Sample production changes and trace them back to approvals and tests.
traps: Programmers should not have access to production.

sections.title: Operational Log Management
sections.summary: New section in the 28th edition: managing operational logs (audit trails) so events can be monitored, investigated and attributed.
points: Logs record type, time, location, source, outcome and identity of parties for each event.
Log types: event, server, system, access, change, availability, threat, database, error and firewall logs.
Log management cycle: collect, generate alerts, store centrally (log server/SIEM), analyse, report concerns, implement action plans.
Secure logs against tampering; centralise them; synchronise time; define retention.
Log review can be a compensating control where segregation of duties is limited.

terms.d: Security information and event management: collects, correlates and alerts on log data.
Chronological record of activities that allows reconstruction of events.

auditor: Check which events are logged, who can alter logs, and whether alerts are reviewed and acted on.
traps: Logs kept on the same server administrators control are not reliable evidence.

sections.title: IT Service Level Management
sections.summary: Covers defining, agreeing and monitoring service levels.
points: SLAs with the business; OLAs between internal teams; underpinning contracts with vendors.
Service catalogue defines services, owners and targets.
Reports must be based on independently measured data.

terms.d: Operational level agreement between internal IT groups supporting an SLA.

auditor: Recalculate SLA metrics from source logs.
traps: Provider self-reported SLA data needs verification.

sections.title: Database Management
sections.summary: Explains DBMS architecture, models and controls.
points: DBMS architecture and data dictionary/directory; metadata types.
Models: hierarchical, network, relational, object, NoSQL; normalisation reduces redundancy.
Controls: restricted direct access, DBA activity logging and review, backup/recovery, integrity constraints, encryption.

terms.d: Organising tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies.
Foreign keys always refer to existing primary keys.

auditor: Review privileged database accounts and how DBA actions are monitored.
traps: The DBA should not review their own activity.

sections.title: Business Impact Analysis
sections.summary: Identifies critical processes and the impact of disruption to set recovery priorities.
points: BIA determines criticality, impact over time, dependencies, RTO and RPO.
Inputs from business process owners through interviews, questionnaires and workshops.
Results drive classification (critical, vital, sensitive, non-critical) and recovery strategy.

terms.d: Maximum tolerable downtime before the business suffers unacceptable harm.

auditor: Check BIA is current and approved by business owners.
traps: BIA comes before choosing recovery strategies.

sections.title: System and Operational Resilience
sections.summary: Covers designing systems to withstand and recover from disruption.
points: Resilience techniques: redundancy, fault tolerance, clustering, RAID, geographically dispersed sites.
RTO drives recovery speed; RPO drives data replication or backup frequency.
Lower RTO/RPO costs more; decisions balance cost against impact.

terms.d: Recovery time objective: maximum acceptable downtime.
Recovery point objective: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

auditor: Check resilience designs meet BIA requirements.
traps: Low RPO needs frequent backups or mirroring; low RTO needs hot sites or high availability.

sections.title: Data Backup, Storage and Restoration
sections.summary: Explains backup schemes, media, offsite storage and restore testing.
points: Full, incremental and differential backups; rotation schemes such as grandfather-father-son.
Backups stored offsite or in separate cloud regions; protected and encrypted.
Restores must be tested regularly; immutable backups help against ransomware.

terms.d: Copies all changes since the last full backup.
Copies changes since the last backup of any type.

auditor: Review restore test results, not just backup job success.
traps: Untested backups give no assurance of recovery.

sections.title: Business Continuity Plan
sections.summary: Covers developing, testing and maintaining the BCP.
points: BCP lifecycle: policy, BIA, strategy, plan, training, testing, maintenance.
Plan content: roles, invocation criteria, communication, recovery procedures, contact lists.
Tests: checklist, walk-through/table-top, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
Senior management approves the plan; it must be reviewed after changes and tests.

terms.d: Discussion-based walk-through of a scenario by the response team.

auditor: Check test results against objectives and that gaps are corrected.
traps: Full interruption tests are the most disruptive and least frequent.

sections.title: Disaster Recovery Plans
sections.summary: Explains recovering IT services after a disaster.
points: Recovery sites: hot, warm, cold, mirrored, mobile, cloud-based, reciprocal agreements.
DRP teams have clear roles; plans are tested and updated.
Recovery strategy is chosen to meet RTO/RPO at acceptable cost.

terms.d: Fully equipped site ready to run within hours.

auditor: Check DR test scope, results and updates to the plan.
traps: Reciprocal agreements are the least reliable recovery option.

sections.title: Information Asset Security Policies, Frameworks, Standards and Guidelines
sections.summary: Covers the security policy framework, ISMS and the roles that govern information security.
points: Security policy approved by senior management sets direction; supported by standards and procedures.
Frameworks: ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, ISO/IEC 27002 controls, NIST CSF.
Roles: board, executive management, CISO, data owners, custodians, users, auditors.

terms.d: Information security management system: a managed, continually improving approach to security.

auditor: Check policy approval, communication and periodic review.
traps: Senior management commitment is the most critical success factor.

sections.title: Physical and Environmental Controls
sections.summary: Explains protecting facilities and equipment from physical and environmental threats.
points: Physical access: badges, biometrics, mantraps, guards, CCTV, visitor logs.
Environmental: UPS, generators, fire detection and suppression, water detection, HVAC, raised floors.
Power issues: blackout, brownout, sag, spike, surge, EMI.

terms.d: Two-door entry where only one door opens at a time, preventing tailgating.

auditor: Inspect facilities and test that alarms and suppression systems are maintained.
traps: Dry-pipe systems reduce accidental water damage; halon is no longer used.

sections.title: Identity and Access Management
sections.summary: Covers identification, authentication, authorisation and managing access through its lifecycle.
points: Least privilege, need to know and segregation of duties guide access design.
Authentication factors: know, have, are; MFA combines different types.
Access models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC; SSO and federation need strong authentication.
Lifecycle: request, approve (by owner), provision, review periodically, revoke promptly.
Biometrics: FAR (security risk), FRR (inconvenience), EER for comparison.

terms.d: Giving users only the access required for their role.
False acceptance rate: impostors accepted.

auditor: Test joiner/mover/leaver processes and periodic access reviews.
traps: Two passwords is not MFA.
Data owners approve access, not IT administrators.

sections.title: Network and Endpoint Security
sections.summary: Explains securing networks and devices with layered controls.
points: Firewalls (packet filter, stateful, application/proxy, next-generation) and DMZ architectures.
IDS/IPS, network segmentation, VPNs, NAC, wireless security.
Endpoint protection: hardening, EDR/anti-malware, patching, device encryption.

terms.d: Screened subnet between the internet and the internal network for public-facing servers.

auditor: Review firewall rule sets for unnecessary or overly permissive rules.
traps: A screened subnet (DMZ) is more secure than a single firewall.

sections.title: Data Loss Prevention
sections.summary: Covers detecting and preventing unauthorised data exfiltration.
points: DLP covers data at rest, in motion and in use (endpoint, network, cloud).
Effective DLP depends on data classification and tuned policies.
Alerts need triage and response processes.

terms.d: Tools and processes that detect and block sensitive data leaving authorised boundaries.

auditor: Check DLP rules map to classification and that alerts are investigated.
traps: Classification must exist before DLP can work well.

sections.title: Data Encryption
sections.summary: Explains symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing and digital signatures.
points: Symmetric (AES): fast, key distribution is the challenge.
Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): public/private keys enable key exchange and signatures.
Hashing provides integrity; digital signatures provide integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.
Key management (generation, storage, rotation, destruction) is critical.

terms.d: Sender cannot deny sending: achieved with the sender’s private key signature.

auditor: Review key management procedures and protection of private keys.
traps: Confidentiality: encrypt with the recipient’s public key.

sections.title: Public Key Infrastructure
sections.summary: Covers certificates, certificate authorities and trust.
points: CA issues certificates; RA verifies identity; CRL/OCSP show revocation.
Certificates bind a public key to an identity; trust chains up to a root CA.
Protecting the CA private key is paramount.

terms.d: Certificate revocation list.

auditor: Check certificate lifecycle management and expiry monitoring.
traps: Compromise of the CA private key undermines all issued certificates.

sections.title: Cloud and Virtualized Environments
sections.summary: Explains cloud service and deployment models, shared responsibility and virtualisation risks.
points: Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS; deployment: public, private, hybrid, community.
Shared responsibility: provider secures the cloud; customer secures configuration, identities and data.
Assurance: SOC reports, certifications, right-to-audit, data location, exit plans.
Virtualisation: protect the hypervisor, control VM sprawl, isolate workloads.

terms.d: Division of security duties between cloud provider and customer.

auditor: Review cloud configurations and IAM, not just the provider’s certificates.
traps: Accountability for data stays with the customer.

sections.title: Mobile, Wireless and Internet of Things Devices
sections.summary: Covers securing mobile devices, wireless networks and IoT.
points: Mobile: MDM, encryption, remote wipe, app control, BYOD policy.
Wireless: strong encryption (WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise), rogue AP detection.
IoT: change defaults, patch firmware, segment networks, inventory devices.

terms.d: Mobile device management.

auditor: Check BYOD policy enforcement and lost-device procedures.
traps: Remote wipe and encryption are key for lost or stolen devices.

sections.title: Security Awareness Training and Programs
sections.summary: Explains building effective security awareness, training and education.
points: Continuum: awareness for all, training for roles, education for specialists.
Needs assessment, targeted content, regular delivery and measured effectiveness (e.g. phishing simulations).

terms.d: Ongoing activities to make people recognise and respond to threats.

auditor: Check completion rates and whether results change behaviour.
traps: Awareness is the best control against social engineering.

sections.title: Information System Attack Methods and Techniques
sections.summary: Covers attackers, motives and common attack techniques.
points: Threat actors: insiders, criminals, hacktivists, nation states.
Attacks: phishing, malware, ransomware, DoS/DDoS, man-in-the-middle, SQL injection, XSS, brute force, social engineering, salami, logic bombs.
Passive attacks (eavesdropping, traffic analysis) are hard to detect.

terms.d: Stealing tiny amounts from many transactions.

auditor: Map controls to the attack techniques most relevant to the organisation.
traps: Encryption is the best control against eavesdropping.

sections.title: Security Testing Tools and Techniques
sections.summary: Explains vulnerability scanning, penetration testing and other security tests.
points: Vulnerability assessments find known weaknesses; penetration tests exploit them to show impact.
Test types: black, white, grey box; internal and external; red/blue/purple teams.
Tests require written authorisation, defined scope and rules of engagement.

terms.d: Agreed scope, limits and timing for a security test.

auditor: Check findings are tracked to remediation.
traps: Never test without written management approval.

sections.title: Security Monitoring Logs, Tools and Techniques
sections.summary: Covers monitoring security events with logs, SIEM and related tools.
points: SIEM correlates logs and raises alerts; SOC teams triage.
Use cases, thresholds and tuning reduce false positives.
Log integrity and time synchronisation matter for investigations.

terms.d: Security operations center that monitors and responds to security events.

auditor: Check alert handling times and evidence of follow-up.
traps: Collecting logs without reviewing them gives little protection.

sections.title: Security Incident Response Management
sections.summary: Explains preparing for and handling security incidents.
points: Phases: preparation, detection/identification, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned.
Roles, escalation paths, communication and legal/regulatory notification are defined in advance.
Incidents are classified by severity to drive response.

terms.d: Limiting the spread and impact of an incident.

auditor: Check plans are tested and lessons learned are implemented.
traps: Containment comes before eradication.

sections.title: Evidence Collection and Forensics
sections.summary: Covers collecting and preserving digital evidence so it is admissible.
points: Identify, preserve, collect, examine, analyse, report.
Work on verified forensic images (hash values), never the original.
Maintain chain of custody; involve legal counsel.

terms.d: Bit-for-bit copy of storage verified by hash.

auditor: Check procedures exist before an incident occurs.
traps: Powering off or browsing a suspect machine can destroy evidence.
